content.text: 646 server tests and 361 browser-app tests pass, with `domain/` still at 100% coverage. Pushing the server half and opening it stacked on #55.

input.command:
git push -q -u origin feat/04-the-request-names-its-start 2>&1 | tail -1; cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-kentgang-git3-katalyst/a73625ea-375b-47a2-b223-9e9fce3d0d66/scratchpad/pr-d2b.md <<'EOF'
**Stacked on #55 (record 0012's amendment, `proposed`). It does not reach `main` before Kent accepts that.**

## What

`GenerateRequest` gains one field, **`start`**, either `replay` or `live`, and the generate route reads it **instead of reading the key**. The key now says only whether a live run is *possible*; the request says which was *asked for*.

| Asked for | Key | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| `replay` | none | the recording plays — as today |
| `replay` | present | **the recording plays** — unreachable before |
| `live` | present | a live run — as today |
| `live` | none | **refused in one sentence**: a receipt of zeroes marked `live`, then words that name what is missing *and say nothing was put in its place* |

- **The default is `replay`**, because a request that did not ask to spend money must never spend it. It is a property of the request's shape, published in the server's own description of itself; it reads no key, no environment and no folder — so it is not the server choosing.
- **A keyed browser is not regressed.** The browser now says which: `start: hasKey ? "live" : "replay"` in `App.tsx` — the expression the route used to compute, moved to the side that knows what was pressed. Behaviour today is identical with and without a key; the first-screen pull request, stacked on this, replaces that expression with the reader's choice.
- **`RecordingSummary` carries the recorded run's `calls`, `seconds` and `dollars`**, read off the recording's own receipt line by one builder the readiness route shares, so the first screen can state what a live run costs before the press. Absent together when a recording has no readable receipt.
- `frontend/src/api/schema.ts` regenerated (`make types`); `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `spec/generation/streaming.md` and the request block in `spec/workbench/streaming-growth.md` (a test compares that block with the code field for field) say who chooses now.

**Pinned by** `test_a_recording_plays_when_the_request_asks_for_one_and_a_key_is_present` (a key really configured, and the model seam asked nothing) and `test_a_live_run_with_no_key_is_refused_in_words` (the recording of that very sentence sitting on disk, unplayed); `test_a_summary_quotes_the_recorded_runs_own_receipt` compares each figure with the line it came from — no number is typed; two `App.test.tsx` cases pin what the browser sends in each state of the key.

Checked by the coordinator: whole server suite 646 passed, `domain/` 100% covered; `mypy`, `ruff` clean; browser app 361 passed, lint and types clean; one cold browser run 14 of 14 — all through the queue.

## Which invariant it satisfies

Record 0012's amended rule — *the server never chooses and never substitutes* — in both directions, and the server half of **INV-workbench.83** (every price and duration the first screen prints came from the server's answer about itself).

**The one shape freeze (R5) is untouched, and proven:** the field is our own HTTP body and never reaches the vendor. The prompt fingerprint is byte for byte the one in `backend/recordings/hormuz.jsonl`'s header, and the fingerprint, wire-schema and nine cassette tests pass with no edit.

## What is deliberately not here — and what is rough

- **The first screen itself** — `Launchpad.tsx` and the four ways to start are the next pull request. Until it lands, a keyed browser still cannot reach the recording: the server now allows it, nothing on screen asks for it yet.
- Stack 07's third value (*a finished generation served back by its id*): the field is shaped for it and does not carry it.
- **A pre-existing test-ordering fault fixed in passing:** `test_health.py` pointed itself at an empty recordings folder through an environment variable, but settings are read once and cached, so whichever of it and `test_replay.py` ran first decided. Its fixture now clears the cache on the way in and out.
- The field's description first typed in the recorded run's receipt figures; it now points at the readiness route, which serves them, so nothing goes stale when the recordings are re-made at the freeze.
- Thirteen existing live tests now say `start="live"` through one helper — they had relied on a key being configured, which the route no longer reads.
- Will conflict, lightly, with #51 in `spec/workbench/streaming-growth.md` and `ARCHITECTURE.md`: second to land rebases and keeps both.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

I built a local branch, `try/04c-all`, that merges the three code pull requests (#50, #52, #56) onto the latest `main`. It typechecks, lints clean and passes 370 browser-app tests. It is not pushed, and I left your checkout on `main`, clean.

## Run it

```bash
cd /Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst
git switch try/04c-all
make dev                      # http://localhost:5173/, Ctrl+C stops everything
# when done:
git switch main
```

Your `.env` stays where it is, so it runs with your key as usual. To see the keyless state, start it with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY= make dev`.

## What to try

| Try | Expect | PR |
|---|---|---|
| Press `?` on the first screen, then press *Watch it build* and press `?` **while the map is still arriving** | The key sheet opens and `Escape` closes it. Both were dead before | #50 |
| Open the recording or any generated map and look at the tiles | Each tile shows only the model's column; the empty user and market columns are gone and no tile changed size. On the curated Hormuz map the hypothesis still shows `model` and `user`, and the Polymarket ending still shows `model` and `market` | #52 |
| Click an arrow and read its *kind* row in the panel | *fires once…* or *holds while the cause holds…*; no domino, no apple on a desk | #52 |
| With your key in, ask the server for the recording (below) | It replays. Before, it was unreachable with a key | #56 |

```bash
# with your key in, the recording now plays when asked for by name:
curl -sN -X POST localhost:8000/api/generate -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"hypothesis":"The Strait of Hormuz is going to open next week.","start":"replay"}' | head -5
# and what a live run cost when it was recorded (calls, seconds, dollars):
curl -s localhost:8000/api/readyz | python3 -m json.tool
```

## What is not in it yet

Three of the things you asked for are still being built, so you won't see them on this branch:

- **The live-status strip** — *nothing new for 23 s*. It is still running; until it lands, a live run is as silent as before.
- **The layout fix** for backwards arrows. It waits on the strip.
- **The unified first screen.** It is still running. Until it lands, nothing on screen offers the recording when your key is in, which is why the check above is a `curl`.

Known rough spot: on the first screen, `?` opens a sheet that still lists map keys that do nothing there.

The two docs pull requests, #51 (records 0023 and 0024) and #55 (record 0012's amendment), are best read on GitHub. They need your acceptance, not a run, and #51 conflicts with the others in two documents, so I left it off this branch.

content.content:
/**
 * The suite's own `test`, and the one thing it holds every browser test to that
 * no assertion inside a test would ever catch.
 *
 * **The browser complains in the log, and a log is not a test.** When too many
 * size observations fall due in one frame, the browser abandons the rest of them
 * and says so — *"ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications"*.
 * The development server forwards it, and it scrolls past among the rest of the
 * output while every test goes on passing. Three of them went past in one run on
 * 2026-09-21 and nothing anywhere went red.
 *
 * That exact message was the root of a real defect in this stack: the drawing
 * library draws nothing it has not measured, so an abandoned notification left a
 * tile invisible and its arrows off the glass for the life of the page
 * (`graph/toFlow.ts` tells the whole story). That harm is prevented at the root
 * now — every tile's box and both ends of every wire are **declared**, so nothing
 * waits to be measured — but two things on screen still read sizes that arrive
 * this way: the rule at the stage's edges and the rules at the panel's. A
 * dropped notification there is a rule that lies until the next change.
 *
 * So: **a test that meets this message fails, and says so in the browser's own
 * words** — unless it has said out loud that it expects one, and why.
 *
 * Every browser test in this folder takes its `test` from here rather than from
 * the library, so that there is no way to write one that quietly does not have
 * this.
 *
 * **Why the page is asked rather than the driver.** The obvious way to catch
 * this is `page.on("pageerror")`, and it does not work: measured on 2026-09-21
 * against a loop caused on purpose, Chromium does not deliver this one to the
 * driver as a page error at all. It is delivered to the page, as an `error`
 * event on `window`, which is how the development server sees it — so that is
 * where this listens, installed before anything else runs. What it finds is kept
 * in the page's own session store rather than in a variable, so that a test that
 * reloads the page does not lose what happened before the reload.
 */

import { test as playwrights } from "@playwright/test";

/** What the browser says when it has abandoned a frame's size notifications. */

34:import { test } from "./theSuite.js";
35:import {
608:test("test_the_mouse_alone_reaches_the_six_things_you_can_do", async ({ page }) => {
669:test("the stored example, opened and edited by keyboard alone", async ({ page }) => {
1058:test("test_this_happened_puts_rows_on_the_rail", async ({ page }) => {

/**
 * The suite's own `test`, and the one thing it holds every browser test to that
 * no assertion inside a test would ever catch.
 *
 * **The browser complains in the log, and a log is not a test.** When too many
 * size observations fall due in one frame, the browser abandons the rest of them
 * and says so — *"ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications"*.
 * The development server forwards it, and it scrolls past among the rest of the
 * output while every test goes on passing. Three of them went past in one run on
 * 2026-09-21 and nothing anywhere went red.
 *
 * That exact message was the root of a real defect in this stack: the drawing
 * library draws nothing it has not measured, so an abandoned notification left a
 * tile invisible and its arrows off the glass for the life of the page
 * (`graph/toFlow.ts` tells the whole story). That harm is prevented at the root
 * now — every tile's box and both ends of every wire are **declared**, so nothing
 * waits to be measured — but two things on screen still read sizes that arrive
 * this way: the rule at the stage's edges and the rules at the panel's. A
 * dropped notification there is a rule that lies until the next change.
 *
 * So: **a test that meets this message fails, and says so in the browser's own
 * words** — unless it has said out loud that it expects one, and why.
 *
 * Every browser test in this folder takes its `test` from here rather than from
 * the library, so that there is no way to write one that quietly does not have
 * this.
 *
 * **Why the page is asked rather than the driver.** The obvious way to catch
 * this is `page.on("pageerror")`, and it does not work: measured on 2026-09-21

 * driver as a page error at all. It is delivered to the page, as an `error`
 * event on `window`, which is how the development server sees it — so that is
 * where this listens, installed before anything else runs. What it finds is kept
 * in the page's own session store rather than in a variable, so that a test that
 * reloads the page does not lose what happened before the reload.
 */

50	/** Read every tile's belief lines off the glass and hold them to the three rules. */
51	async function everyLineIsWhole(page: Page): Promise<void> {
52	  const tiles = await page.$$eval(".react-flow__node .tile", (found) =>
53	    found.map((tile) => {
54	      const row = tile.querySelector(".tile__beliefs")?.getBoundingClientRect();
55	      // The ink of one belief line: every piece of text in it that is really

60	          .filter((piece) => piece.children.length === 0 && piece.textContent?.trim())
61	          .map((piece) => piece.getBoundingClientRect())
62	          .filter((box) => box.width > 2 && box.height > 2);
63	        return {
64	          owner: chip.getAttribute("data-owner"),
65	          left: Math.min(...drawn.map((box) => box.left)),
66	          right: Math.max(...drawn.map((box) => box.right)),
67	          top: Math.min(...drawn.map((box) => box.top)),
68	          bottom: Math.max(...drawn.map((box) => box.bottom)),

70	      });

and on the one tile holding a venue's number, two lines printed over each other.

range. It is now as wide as 'market' and no wider.

## Draft pull request body

### What

One first screen. Kent ran the app with his real key and met a screen nobody had designed for him: every card called a model, the committed recording was unreachable, and a live run gave no idea what it would cost before he pressed. *"Why do i need to blank out the anthropic key?"* · *"How can i test out all the functionality if I run it with a valid anthropic key?"*

What changes between a reader with a key and one without is only what is enabled and the reason printed beside what is not.

What a live run costs and how long it takes is on screen **before the press**, read off the recorded run's own receipt as `GET /api/readyz` carries it, printed with the day it was measured, and absent with a reason where no recording carries a readable receipt. A sentence of your own says it is a live run too, and says honestly that its own price is not known until it has run.

The two unpressable *Explore / Verify* rows are gone.

### Which invariant it satisfies

- **INV-workbench.82** — for every way to start, and for both states of `model_key_present`, the same ways are drawn, in the same order, with the same words; a way that cannot be taken is drawn disabled with the reason beside itself. - **INV-workbench.83** — every duration and every price came from the server's answer about itself and is printed with the day it was measured. Checked by three render tests and one source check; the expected figures are read off `backend/recordings/hormuz.jsonl` rather than typed into a fixture.
- **Record 0012, amended 2026-09-21** — a reader choosing a recording is not a fallback; the server never chooses and never substitutes.
- **Red team item 5(e)** — row 4 no longer carries no price while row 3 quotes one.

### What is deliberately not here

- **No `?` hook-up and no key sheet.** `?` does nothing on the first screen on this base; `fix/04-the-question-mark` (#50) adds it, and a line saying so becomes true only once this is rebased over it.
- **No help page.** It rides after this, with the words already drafted.
- **No duration on the recording row.** It could be worked out from the event count times the replay pace, and neither is served — a duration this screen worked out itself would break INV-workbench.83.
- **No figures for the three unrecorded sentences.** Printing another example's price beside the run somebody is about to start is close enough to a typed-in number to be refused on purpose.
- **No mode switch, no product tour, no first-run hints, no modal.** Each way says what it is.
- **No server change.** `GenerateRequest.start` and `RecordingSummary`'s three receipt fields landed in the pull request under this one.</result>

"""Working the likelihoods through a map: what a world is, and how it is computed.

A branch is a list of edits; a world is what those edits do to the numbers. This
file is the arithmetic in between. It takes the map a fold left behind, the
values that fold fixed, a day to start from and a seed, and gives back one
`World`: a likelihood for every claim on the day that claim is judged, a
likelihood for every day in between, a named state for every one of those days,
and a plain sentence for anything the reader should be told.

**Two loops, because there are two kinds of not-knowing.**

* *How the dice fall.* The strait either opens or it does not. That is already
  inside the likelihood: it is the share of worlds in which the claim came out
  true.
* *How sure we are of the numbers we put in.* Every prior on the map was
  elicited, and **every arrow's push was written down by somebody with more or
  less to go on**. A different but equally defensible set of those numbers would
  give a different answer. **That** is the range.

So the outer loop draws 2 000 **versions of the map** — each one a coherent set
of numbers this model would have stood behind — and the inner loop runs 8
**worlds** under each. The range is the middle 80% across versions once the
coin-flip noise has been subtracted out. A wide range means "we are not sure what
number to give you; more homework would move it", never "the event is more
volatile".

**What this file must never do**

- Never report the spread of the coin flips as the range. Run more worlds and
  that number shrinks, which makes it a statement about the machine rather than
  about the map. The inner noise is subtracted with the law of total variance,
  and a test freezes every prior at a point and demands a band of no width.
- Never let the stream that picks the versions depend on the branch. A base world
  and a branch world built from one seed must try the *same* 2 000 versions, or
  every comparison between them is the user's edit plus a wash of noise. Each
  claim's prior and each arrow's push get a stream of their own, keyed by the seed
  and by that thing's own identifier, so adding a claim or an arrow cannot shift
  what any other one drew.
- Never let a drawn push change the *shape* of the map. Which arrows oppose a
  supposition, and the day one of them undermines it, are read off the strength
  the map states — the same answer in every version, because a retraction is one
  record on one world and cannot be true in version 7 and false in version 8.
  A drawn push decides only how hard that arrow shoves inside its own version.
- Never store how wide an arrow's push is. It is derived from where the arrow came
  from, every time, and there is no `strength_lo` and no `strength_hi`.
- Never model a supposition as a large baseline the arrows argue with. While a
  supposition holds the claim is true in **every** draw, and the tile shows a word
  where a number would mislead.
- Never fit a stated likelihood and its range on the probability scale. The two
  halves are fitted separately on the log-odds scale — the scale the pushes add
  on — which honours all three stated numbers exactly and can never leave 0 to 1.
- No clock, no network, no global random state. Every random number comes from
  the one `seed` argument, so the same map, branch and seed give the same world
  on any machine.
- Never unroll a feedback arrow. A market feeding back on the world is carried as
  data and set aside here exactly as the map's own loop check sets it aside; a
  later stack works it through over time.
"""

def _version_priors(claim: Proposition, seed: int, versions: int) -> Numbers:
    """Draw one likelihood per version for one claim's prior.

    The draws are spread evenly over the curve rather than left to clump — a Latin
    hypercube, which here is one stratified column per claim. Each claim's column
    comes from the seed and the claim's own identifier and from nothing else, which
    is what makes a base world and a branch world share their versions: adding a
    claim to the map cannot shift the numbers drawn for any other.

    Args:
        claim: The claim whose prior is being drawn.
        seed: The one number every draw comes from.
        versions: How many versions to draw.

    Returns:
        One likelihood per version.
    """
    drawer = numpy.random.default_rng([seed, PARAMS_STREAM, _stream_key(claim.id)])
    strata = (drawer.permutation(versions) + drawer.random(versions)) / versions
    steps = _standard_normal_quantile(strata)
    below, above = _fitted_halves(claim.prior)
    middle = float(_log_odds(numpy.array(claim.prior.p)))
    return _likelihood_of(middle + steps * numpy.where(steps < 0.0, below, above))


def _version_strengths(
    arrow: Link, seed: int, versions: int, spreads: Mapping[Provenance, float]
) -> Numbers:
    """Draw one push per version for one arrow, as wide as where it came from says.

    The same stratified draw the priors get — spread evenly over the curve rather
    than left to clump — and, like theirs, the numbers come from the seed and the
    arrow's **own** identifier and from nothing else. So adding an arrow cannot
    shift what another arrow drew, and version 7 of a base world and version 7 of
    a branch world push exactly as hard as each other along every arrow the two
    maps share.

    The draw is on the log-odds scale, because that is the scale a push is already
    written in: a spread of four tenths is four tenths of a log-odds unit, whatever
    the push itself happens to be. A weakly-backed push can therefore come out the
    other way round in some versions, and that is the honest reading — *we do not
    know which way this one goes* is most of what `asserted` means.

    Args:
        arrow: The arrow whose push is being drawn.
        seed: The one number every draw comes from.
        versions: How many versions to draw.
        spreads: How wide each kind of arrow's push is drawn.

    Returns:
        One push per version.
    """
    drawer = numpy.random.default_rng([seed, STRENGTHS_STREAM, _stream_key(arrow.id)])
    strata = (drawer.permutation(versions) + drawer.random(versions)) / versions
    steps = _standard_normal_quantile(strata)
    drawn: Numbers = arrow.strength + steps * spreads[arrow.provenance]
    return drawn

def _version_priors(claim: Proposition, seed: int, versions: int) -> Numbers:
    """Draw one likelihood per version for one claim's prior.

    The draws are spread evenly over the curve rather than left to clump — a Latin
    hypercube, which here is one stratified column per claim. Each claim's column
    comes from the seed and the claim's own identifier and from nothing else, which
    is what makes a base world and a branch world share their versions: adding a
    claim to the map cannot shift the numbers drawn for any other.

    Args:
        claim: The claim whose prior is being drawn.
        seed: The one number every draw comes from.
        versions: How many versions to draw.

    Returns:
        One likelihood per version.
    """
    drawer = numpy.random.default_rng([seed, PARAMS_STREAM, _stream_key(claim.id)])
    strata = (drawer.permutation(versions) + drawer.random(versions)) / versions
    steps = _standard_normal_quantile(strata)
    below, above = _fitted_halves(claim.prior)
    middle = float(_log_odds(numpy.array(claim.prior.p)))
    return _likelihood_of(middle + steps * numpy.where(steps < 0.0, below, above))


def _version_strengths(
    arrow: Link, seed: int, versions: int, spreads: Mapping[Provenance, float]
) -> Numbers:
    """Draw one push per version for one arrow, as wide as where it came from says.

    The same stratified draw the priors get — spread evenly over the curve rather
    than left to clump — and, like theirs, the numbers come from the seed and the
    arrow's **own** identifier and from nothing else. So adding an arrow cannot
    shift what another arrow drew, and version 7 of a base world and version 7 of
    a branch world push exactly as hard as each other along every arrow the two
    maps share.

    The draw is on the log-odds scale, because that is the scale a push is already
    written in: a spread of four tenths is four tenths of a log-odds unit, whatever
    the push itself happens to be. A weakly-backed push can therefore come out the
    other way round in some versions, and that is the honest reading — *we do not
    know which way this one goes* is most of what `asserted` means.

    Args:
        arrow: The arrow whose push is being drawn.
        seed: The one number every draw comes from.
        versions: How many versions to draw.
        spreads: How wide each kind of arrow's push is drawn.

    Returns:
        One push per version.
    """
    drawer = numpy.random.default_rng([seed, STRENGTHS_STREAM, _stream_key(arrow.id)])
    strata = (drawer.permutation(versions) + drawer.random(versions)) / versions
    steps = _standard_normal_quantile(strata)
    drawn: Numbers = arrow.strength + steps * spreads[arrow.provenance]
    return drawn

content.text:
Here is the engine answer while the combined branch runs through the queue. This is how the code on `main` works today; stack 05's records change the inner arithmetic.

## The 2 000 versions are arithmetic, not model calls

It is a deterministic, seeded simulation in `backend/src/katalyst/domain/propagation.py`. That module imports `numpy` and `networkx` and nothing that can reach a network. Its docstring states the rule: *no clock, no network, no global random state*. The same map, branch and seed give the same numbers on any machine, and the project notes measured a world at about 65 ms. No LLM call is made for any of the 2 000.

The model is called only to build the map. The recorded Hormuz run made 29 calls for 18 claims.

## How it produces the number and the range

The model's output is the input. For each claim it states a likelihood with a low and a high. For each arrow it states a push, a delay, a shape and a kind. Our pipeline, not the model, stamps each arrow with where it came from (`documented`, `argued`, `asserted`, and so on). The engine then runs two nested loops, because there are two kinds of uncertainty:

| Loop | What varies | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Outer: 2 000 versions of the map** | Each claim's prior is redrawn inside the range the model stated. Each arrow's push is redrawn as widely as its backing allows: ±0.15 log-odds for `documented`, 0.40 for `argued`, 0.60 for `asserted` | How sure are we of the numbers we put in? |
| **Inner: 8 worlds per version** | Coin flips: does each claim come true, given its causes and their timing | How do the dice fall? |

- **The likelihood** (`.40`) is the share of worlds in which the claim came true.
- **The range** (`.24–.56`) is the middle 80% across the 2 000 versions, after the coin-flip noise is subtracted out. A wide range therefore means "better homework would move this number". It never means "the event is volatile". A test pins this by freezing every input at a point and demanding a range of zero width.

Two details make edits comparable:

- The draws are stratified, not naive random, so 2 000 versions cover the curve evenly.
- Each claim and arrow draws from its own stream, keyed by the seed and its own identifier. When you add a supposition, the base world and the branch world try the same 2 000 versions. The difference you see is your edit, not resampling noise.

One caveat the note itself prints: *uncalibrated*. The 80% is internal consistency, eight in ten of the versions this map could defensibly be. No claim has resolved yet, so nobody has checked whether that 8-in-10 holds up. The width also starts from the model's own stated ranges and our per-provenance spreads, which are judgement calls, not measurements.

I'll post again when `try/04c-next` has passed and is ready to fast-forward.

**You are a READ-ONLY analyst on Katalyst, on Opus.** You change nothing in the repository except the ONE plan file named below. It holds the run strip (`frontend/src/components/RunStrip.tsx`, `frontend/src/a11y/growth.ts`), the first screen, and `GenerateRequest.start`. Server: `backend/src/katalyst/api/generate.py`, `engine/grow.py`, `engine/following.py`, `engine/client.py`, `engine/events.py`, `engine/replay.py`, `engine/outcome.py`, `engine/prompt.py`, `settings.py`; tests' cassettes `backend/tests/conftest.py`.

## Kent's words (2026-09-22) — the assignment

> For clicking the pre-built "The strait of Hormuz is going to open next week card" on the webpage UI, it's very slow, and there still isn't the bottom status bar informing me what's happening. In any case, if there are computations that are slowing this down, could we please simplify those so that the interactive experience is snappier? There should also be better interactivity or updates for the user to understand what's happening, even if it takes a while for the elements to begin appearing on screen. If something is similarly affecting the dynamic, real live use case, that should be improved as well. Generally, the user should get instant feedback that something is happening, like a timer ticking up, and mirroring back explanations to the user what's happening. Generally, there should only be a few seconds between things happening for real on the UI if possible. For example, if we could see the different things that the llm is proposing even if the events are rejected, that'd be helpful.

**What the coordinator already knows:** he pressed that card with his key set on a branch where a key means LIVE, so he was waiting on the model (~23 s to the first proposal, then 50–110 s a round), not on computation. The run strip (a sentence plus *nothing new for N s*) and a recording reachable with a key exist on `try/04c-next` and he has not seen them yet. **So the open problem is the live run: between proposals nothing real happens on screen for about a minute, and he wants a few seconds.**

1. **Where the time goes, measured.** From the four kept runs in `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/backend/.runs/*.json` (each has a `transcript`, a `receipt`, `events`, `seconds`) and the two eval logs `/Users/kentgang/git3/katalyst/plans/logs/eval-hormuz-medium.log` and `eval-hormuz.log`: seconds per call, calls per round, how much of a call is search versus thinking versus writing if the transcript can say, output tokens per call, gaps between events. Candidates to weigh — (a) a ninth *kind* of event, explicitly ephemeral: sent live, never written to a recording or a transcript, never invented by a replay, shown only in the strip and never on the map; (b) the coarse version only: one `asking` event per round naming the claims in flight; (c) a second channel beside the stream; (d) nothing on the wire, better words from what the browser already has. Kent's disgust veto still stands: nothing spins; and *every state traces to an input, a rule or a source* — activity text must be the vendor's own words or ours about a fact, never invented progress.
4. **Refusals.** He asks to see what the model proposes *even if rejected*. `proposal_rejected` already streams and the panel already lists refusals. Find out what he would actually have seen and when: does the strip say a refusal arrived, in the validator's words? Is there anything proposed that is NOT shown (a proposal retried inside one call? a call that returned nothing usable?) — `grow.py`, `following.py`, `outcome.py`.
5. **Making the live run itself faster** — levers, each with the evidence we already hold and what it would cost in quality: effort (`medium` today, R34; the eval scored 7 of 8 at `medium` against 8 of 8 at the recorder's effort), `at_once` (3 today, `outcome.py` ~311), search limits per call, output-token ceiling, prompt caching (the receipt has `cache_read`), first round shape (could the first call ask for fewer/lighter claims so something lands in under ten seconds?). **Any lever that changes what the model is asked moves the prompt fingerprint — say which do and which do not**, because R5 holds fingerprint changes for one freeze and that is Kent's to waive. |---|---|

| Any map building | One strip at the foot saying what the run is doing and naming which claim it is working on. On a live run it also shows *nothing new for N s*, counting up |

questions.question: How should tile kinds (hypothesis vs tradeable outcome vs ordinary event) use colour? Today kind is carried by SHAPE only, because the colour law gives hue to money direction (blue/amber) and branches (violet/teal/rose/slate).

options.label: Accent + one new hue (Recommended)
options.description: Hypothesis: the teal accent it already borrows, made stronger (outline, kind label, a faint wash). Tradeable outcome: ONE new hue on its outline, cut corner and kind label only, never on a number. Ordinary events stay neutral so the two ends of the map stand out. Amends the colour law with a dated line: hue may also say what kind of tile this is; shape still carries it too, so greyscale still reads. The agent picks the hue by measured contrast and distance from the six in use, and shows you pictures.

options.label: No new hue, stronger contrast
options.description: Keep the colour law untouched. Hypothesis gets the stronger teal treatment; tradeable outcomes get a brighter raised surface, a heavier rule and a bolder kind label in plain text colour. Safest and smallest, but it is brightness and weight rather than colour, so it may not be what you meant.

options.label: A hue per kind
options.description: Hypothesis, event, tradeable outcome and dead end each get their own hue. The most colourful, and the furthest from the colour law: it leaves only the branch hues and blue/amber unspent-looking, risks a tile being read as a branch or a direction, and is the closest of the three to a template look.

questions.question: When the whole batch is verified, who merges it? Records 0023, 0024 and the amendment to 0012 are still marked proposed, and the code is built on them.

options.label: You land it; records accepted (Recommended)
options.description: I rebase the branches into one ordered batch, wait for the build's checks, and land each with scripts/land.sh. Merging counts as you accepting records 0023, 0024 and 0012's amendment; I flip their status lines to accepted in the same batch and date it. I tell you what landed and why before you have to ask.

options.label: Prepare it; I press merge

Both answers are recorded as decisions R42 and R43. The colour lane is now running on Opus.

## The experience with and without a key

Yes. It's built, I've verified it, and it's on `try/04c-next`. It is not opened as a pull request yet.

The first screen now offers the same four ways to start, in the same order and the same words, whether or not a key is set. The key only changes which ones are enabled, and a disabled one says why beside itself.

| Way | No key | Key |
|---|---|---|
| 1 · Open the map | pressable | pressable |
| 2 · Watch the recording (badged *replay*) | pressable | **pressable** (it was unreachable with a key before) |
| 3 · Run it live, with what the recorded run cost stated before the press | drawn, disabled, reason shown | pressable |
| 4 · Build the map from your own sentence | disabled, same reason | pressable |

Underneath, each press names `replay` or `live` and the server does what it was asked; it no longer reads the key to choose. A new component test checks that both states of the key draw the same ways in the same words.

**One defect is still open.** The replay badge under a map still says *"No model key is configured, so this map is a recording"*. That is false when you have a key and chose the recording. I'll fix it in the batch.

## Colour

The colour lane is building your choice:

- **Hypothesis:** the teal accent it already borrows, made stronger.
- **Tradeable outcomes:** one new hue, on the outline, the cut corner and the kind label only. It never touches a number.

The agent has to pick the hue by measurement: distance from the six hues already in use, and contrast in both themes. It has been told that a green that reads as "profit" is suspect on a finance screen. It will bring you two or three candidate hues as pictures and build the one it recommends. It also writes the dated amendment to the colour law, and shape keeps carrying kind too, so greyscale still reads.

## Merging

You chose that I land the batch and that merging is acceptance. When everything is verified I'll rebase it into one ordered batch, wait for the checks, and land it with `land.sh`. In the same batch I'll flip records 0023, 0024 and 0012's amendment to `accepted`, and I'll tell you what landed.

## 2. The designs

### (a) The tile — recommended: **one rule, no guard**

> **The model's column is always drawn. The reader's and the venue's are drawn when they hold a number.**

```
 before                                  after
 ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ event         resolves Oct 31│        │ event         resolves Oct 31│
 │ Lloyd's war-risk insurance   │        │ Lloyd's war-risk insurance   │
 │ premium … falls below 0.4%.  │        │ premium … falls below 0.4%.  │
 │ ─────────────────────────────│        │ ─────────────────────────────│
 │ model  │ user  │ market      │        │ model                        │
 │ .40    │ —     │ no          │        │ ▬ .40                        │
 │.25–.56 │add yrs│ market      │        │ .25–.56                      │
 └──────────────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────────┘
```

**On screen:** the map loses 36 dead cells on a generated run and reads as numbers rather than apologies. **In code:** ~15 lines in `Tile.tsx:305–314`, one grid rule in `tile.css:134–145` (`grid-auto-flow: column; justify-content: start`), and the text of `tiles-ports-wires.md:94` and its *states of a chip* table. **Cost:** near zero. **Risk:** none I can find — the height constant makes it layout-neutral and the fin

**Where the absences go: nowhere new.** `Inspector.tsx:637–642` already draws `user` and `market` rows whatever they hold, and `:230–235` prints each absence's own reason — *no venue quotes this claim* — as INV-workbench.53 requires. No word changes; the tile stops repeating them down a column.

**How a reader discovers they can add their own number.** The panel's `user` row becomes the control: the dash is replaced by a button reading **My own number** — the vocabulary's own words (`vocabulary.md:86`) — opening the form `InterventionPanel` already has (`BranchPanel.tsx:589–646`). A real way in where today there is a dead span, and one component rather than two.

*Rejected:* a hairline placeholder column (keeps the clutter, adds a rule); collapsing only `user` (needs a per-kind guard, and R11 gives a market ending a better answer).

### (b) The panel — recommended: **three always, the rest folded, the teaching behind a word**

Always: the head; **Beliefs**; **What your edit did**; one line of **Resolves** (date · judge). Folded, each a closed `<button aria-expanded>` with a one-line summary: *Resolves in full* · *Base rate* · *Evidence (2)* · *Why this number* · *Sources* · *Where it came from* · *Run details* (R16). Deleted outright: *Where it sits* (105 words → a glossary entry), the decomposition's closing paragraph (44 words), *Lines t

### (c) The word that explains itself — recommended: **it unfolds in place; nothing new opens over the map**

**The tension.** PRD anti-pattern 9 and UX-10 forbid modals; `VR2` forbids a pop-up; the panel's empty state says *"Nothing in this product opens over the map."* **That sentence is already false** — the command palette (`commandPalette.css:13–19`) and the key sheet (`shortcutsSheet.css:10–24`) both sit `position: absolute; z-index: 40` over it, and `keyboard/focusRing.ts:1–13` already writes the real rule down: *noth

| Option | Verdict |
|---|---|
| A true modal, with a scrim | No. It is the named veto and it steals the map. |
| A popover anchored to the term | No. A fourth floating surface, and it needs its own dismissal and placement rules. |
| **The entry unfolds in place, under the line the word is on** | **Recommended.** No overlay, no focus trap, no Escape, no return of focus — it is a disclosure, so the keyboard and the screen reader get it free (`aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`). |
| A Help page the term links to | No. It leaves the map, and analyst UD owns the tutorial. |

**The one rule, in words:** *A word this product invented is drawn with a dotted underline and is a button; pressing it unfolds that word's definition beneath the line it is on, and pressing it again folds it. It never opens on a tile, because a tile's height is reserved before the browser draws one.* That last clause is not a special case — it is `geometry.ts`'s existing promise, and it keeps UX-1's *detail lives in

**One file owns the glossary.** `frontend/src/words/glossary.ts`: one entry per term, `{ word, oneLine, inFull, seeAlso }`, in the shape `absence.ts` already uses. `spec/vocabulary.md` stays the source of truth for **which** words exist and cites the file by path, exactly as chapters cite `docs/worked-numbers.txt`; a test reads the *Interface words* table and its headwords and fails when a word has no entry or an ent

I couldn't reproduce the overlap in your picture on `try/04c-next`. Looking for it turned up a related bug that I have now handed to an agent. I'll build a fresh test branch for you once everything below is verified.

## The overlap in your picture

On the commit you're running, I tried four states and the `model` and `market` lines stack correctly in all of them:

- the base map zoomed out
- the *Iran is struck* branch open
- the Polymarket tile selected
- zoomed out again with the branch open

Your picture matches the old stylesheet, so the likely cause is that `make dev` was started on `try/04c-all` and is still serving that CSS after the `git switch`. Please restart `make dev` and hard-refresh. If the overlap is still there after that, tell me which map it is and whether a branch is open, because then it is a case I haven't found.

**The related bug.** With the branch open, the engine prints three-digit numbers such as `.074  .029–.13`. Zoomed out, those run past the tile's right edge on the Lloyd's tile and the hypothesis. My earlier fix only made room for two-digit numbers. The worst-case line needs about 272 px and a tile's row is 256 px wide, so no amount of trimming makes it fit. The range has to be allowed onto its own line, inside a tile height that is fixed before anything is drawn. An Opus agent is fixing that on #52 and extending the browser test to run with the branch open.

## What's running

| Lane | What | Stacked on |
|---|---|---|
| **Panel switch** | Buttons at the top of the right-hand panel to switch between its parts. Clicking a card brings its details to the top, which makes it work during a replay too. Today a click does select the card, but its details render at the bottom of the column, below the fold, so it looks like nothing happened. | run strip |
| **Kind colour** | The hypothesis keeps teal, tradeable outcomes get one new colour, and you get candidate pictures. | #52 |
| **Far-tile ranges** | The three-digit overflow above. | #52 |
| **The settle** | Stops arrows pointing backwards during a run and tidies the map once when the run ends. | run strip |
| **Live-feedback analyst** | Measures where the time in a live run goes and what the server could honestly report every few seconds. Read-only. | none |

I told the stacks 05/06 session that the panel is being restructured, since that session owns folding the sections inside the details view.

## The next test branch

When those lanes report, I'll verify each and build `try/04c-3` on the latest `main` with everything merged. I'll run the full unit and browser suites on it, the same way I checked `try/04c-next`, and then give you the branch name.

The live-feedback build comes after the analyst reports. It will bring me a few questions for you first, because putting the model's activity on the wire changes two decisions you have already made. That work will probably go into a later test branch so it doesn't hold up this one.

The replay badge under a map still says no key is configured when you chose the recording with a key set; that fix is going into the batch.

# A destination is where a person wants the story to get to, not
            # somewhere to grow from, so it never joins the frontier.
            yield its_outcome.model_copy(update={"frontier": tuple(walk.frontier)})

    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=caps.at_once) as pool:
        while not walk.stopped and walk.frontier:
            if len(graph.propositions) >= caps.claims:
                walk.the_map_is_full()
                break

            # A round is sized to the room the map has left, not only to how many
            # lines may be asked about at once: three questions in flight bring
            # three claims back, and a cap read once a round is a cap a round
            # steps over (2026-09-20).
            room = caps.claims - len(graph.propositions)
            asking = list(walk.frontier[: min(caps.at_once, room)])
            walk.watch(answerer)
            answers = _ask_about_each(
                pool,
                graph,
                asking,
                target=target,
                answerer=answerer,
                on=on,
                searches_left=caps.searches - walk.receipt.searches,
            )
            # **Every answer of the round is on the bill before any of them is
            # folded.** They were all asked and all billed together, so an
            # exception inside one fold used to take the rest off the receipt
            # (Kent, 2026-09-21).
            walk.bill(answers)
            waiting = list(zip(asking, answers, strict=True))
            while waiting:
                claim_id, answer = waiting.pop(0)
                graph, outcome = walk.fold(graph, claim_id, answer)
                try:
                    yield outcome.model_copy(update={"frontier": tuple(walk.frontier)})
                except GeneratorExit:
                    # The reader went away mid-round. Every call of this round was
                    # made and billed before the first of them was folded, so the
                    # rest are folded here — nobody will see them, and they are
                    # still owed to the working and to the bill (2026-09-20).
                    for left_over, its_answer in waiting:
                        graph, its_outcome = walk.fold(graph, left_over, its_answer)
                        if never_seen is not None:
                            never_seen(its_outcome)
                    raise

questions.question: During a live run, may the server send the browser what the model is doing right now (its web searches and what they found) as a line that is shown and then forgotten: never saved in a recording, never replayed?

options.label: Yes, shown live only (Recommended)
options.description: The foot reads e.g.: live · Working on what follows from "war-risk premiums fall below 0.4%" · searching the web: "Lloyd's JWC Hormuz premium 2026" · nothing new for 14 s, and the search line changes every few seconds. The words are the model's own queries and result titles, nothing invented. A replay of the same map shows the sentence and no search line, the same kind of difference you already accepted for the seconds counter. It amends record 0023's 'no ninth event' and the rule that the stream is exactly eight events; it does not touch the prompt, the cassettes or any recording, so the freeze (R5) stands. This is the only option that gets to 'a few seconds between things'.

options.label: Only name what was asked
options.description: A smaller step: once per round the strip names the claims the model was just asked about. Honest and cheap, but it changes about once a minute, not every few seconds.

options.label: Nothing new on the wire
options.description: Keep record 0023 as written: the sentence and the counting seconds only. Live runs stay about a minute between real changes.

questions.question: A round asks the model about up to three claims at once, then waits for the slowest before showing any of them. Should each claim appear as soon as its own call returns?

options.label: Yes, as each returns (Recommended)
options.description: Measured on your kept Verify run: one round's calls took 131, 44 and 65 s, and today all three claims appear at 131 s. This way they appear at 44, 65 and 131 s. About 48 s less dead screen per round at medium effort. Costs nothing and changes no prompt. It re-orders the 'bill every answer of the round before folding any' rule you set on 2026-09-21, so the build keeps that promise another way: each call is billed the moment it returns, before it is folded.

options.label: Keep rounds together
options.description: Leave it as it is: simpler to reason about, slower to look at.

options.description: Stay at medium (R34). Live runs keep their current length; only the feedback improves.

options.label: Just switch to low
options.description: Make low the development default without measuring. Fastest, and blind: medium already loses one of eight checks.

questions.question: Should the model's summarised thinking also appear on the strip while it works?

## 5. What waits on Kent — four questions

1. **May the wire carry one line that is never written down?** *Hormuz:* the foot reads `live · Working on what follows from "war-risk premiums fall below 0.4%" · searching the web: "Lloyd's JWC Hormuz premium 2026" · nothing new for 14 s`, and the search line changes every few seconds. A replay of the same map shows the sentence and no search line. **Recommended: yes** — the only way to reach *a few seconds*, and the replay difference is the one ADR-0023 already accepted for the seconds counter.
2. **Should a round's answers reach the screen as each call finishes, not all three when the slowest does?** *Hormuz:* that run's second round was 131/44/65 s — today all three claims appear at 131 s, this way at 44, 65 and 131 s. Same map, same order, same seed. It re-orders the billing you fixed on 2026-09-21, so it is yours to say. **Recommended: yes** — half a session, 193 s of dead screen off one run.
3. **May we spend about a dollar measuring what `low` effort costs in quality?** *Hormuz:* `make eval ONLY=hormuz EFFORT=low CAP=5`, ~11 minutes. Thinking is 68% of what the model writes at `medium`, so this is the one lever that could halve the wait rather than hide it. **Recommended: measure, then decide** — `medium` already loses one of eight checks.
4. **Should the model's summarised thinking go on the strip too?** *Hormuz:* a third line, in its words, saying what it is weighing; it needs `thinking.display: "summarized"` on the live request only. **Recommended: not in round one** — it is the one text here about the model's mind rather than about a fact.

EOF

# RECORDER SENDS NOTHING. `EFFORT=as-recorded` sends nothing too, for the day you
# want the scorecard of the maps a reviewer with no key is shown. Which model
# answers is unchanged: KATALYST_MODEL, `claude-sonnet-5` unless you say otherwise.
#
# The same three flags as `record-demo`, meaning the same three things. CAP can
# only lower the $15 hard stop written in code, never lift it — and it bounds the
# WHOLE ROUND, not each case: one running total is carried from case to case, each
# is handed what is left, and a case there is nothing left for is not started. The
# scorecard says which ones those were. Which model answers is the KATALYST_MODEL
# setting and nothing else, so the bill and the scorecard's own column can never
# name two different models.
#
# It prints a scorecard, writes one row per case into `evals/runs/<date>.tsv`, and
# exits non-zero if any check did not hold or if the round ran out of money before
# it reached every case. **Every run is kept under `backend/.runs/` whatever it
# scores**, exactly as a recorded run is.
#
# It is deliberately **not** in the build: it costs money, it needs a key, and
# the same prompt scores slightly differently twice — so a merge would be blocked
# by a model's mood. The build's check on the model boundary is the recorded
# exchanges under `backend/tests/cassettes/`, and nothing else.

eval: ## Score what the language model proposes against saved examples. Spends money; needs a key
	cd backend && PYTHONPATH=.. uv run python -m evals.run \
		$(if $(ONLY),--only $(ONLY),) $(if $(CAP),--cap $(CAP),) \
		$(if $(EFFORT),--effort $(EFFORT),)

# per example, one JSON object per line. It is the only thing that ever writes
# one — a hand-edited recording is a piece of state that traces to nobody.
#

Your four answers are recorded as R44–R47 and three Opus lanes are building them now. The paid low-effort probe is prepared but not run, because what I told you when you approved it was wrong.

## The probe — I got one thing wrong

When you approved the probe I said `make eval` reads your key from `.env` by itself and that I'd never read that file. That is not true. `make eval` runs inside `backend/`, and the settings only load `.env` from the working directory, so your root `.env` is never seen. The earlier paid runs worked because the coordinator's script pulled the key line out of `.env` into a variable, never printed it, and scrubbed it from the log.

You said yes to something I described wrongly, so I have prepared the run and not started it. The script is `plans/scripts/run-eval-hormuz-low.sh`. It runs against a clean worktree of `main`, stops at $5, and saves the kept run outside any worktree. Pick one:

- **You run it yourself.** Put `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in your shell and run `bash plans/scripts/run-eval-hormuz-low.sh`. The script uses your shell's key and never opens `.env`.
- **I run it as-is.** The script reads that one line from `.env`, exactly as the medium-effort run did, and I put it through the queue.

Either way it should cost about $1 and take about 11 minutes. I'll bring you the scorecard next to medium's 7 of 8 and the recorder's 8 of 8.

## What your four answers started

- **Answers as they land (R45).** Each claim appears when its own model call returns, not when the slowest call in the round does. Every call is billed the moment it returns, which keeps your rule from yesterday that a paid call never drops off the receipt.
- **The model says what it is doing (R44, R47).** The server sends the model's own search queries, what those searches found, and its summarised thinking. None of this is recorded or replayed.
  - The agent must check the model vendor's streaming API against its documentation. It cannot make a live call, so it has to tell me which facts rest on the docs alone.
  - It must also prove that the recorder's request stays byte-identical to today's.
  - It is writing decision record 0027 for this. The analyst had called the record 0024, but that number is taken.
- **The strip says it.** The browser half of the above. It is built to a shapes sheet I wrote, so the server and browser halves agree before they meet.

Still running from before: the settle, the panel switcher, the tradeable-tile colour, and the three-digit range fix on #52.

## What happens next

input.summary: Settle: nearest free row, one small follow-up
input.message:
Coordinator here — verified: 202 graph and stream tests pass, types clean, your pictures read left to right. Good, honest report. One follow-up, same worktree and branch, add commits (nothing is pushed yet, but do not rewrite what is there):

1. **Build the refinement you named: a tile whose row is taken in its new column slides to the NEAREST free row, not the first free one below.** Your own measurement is the reason — on Kent's Verify run the Brent tile goes 392 px down when a free row sat 48 px up, and a tile a reader is watching should travel as little as it can. Ties go down (reading order). A reserved rectangle counts as free room only if that is what your 48 px case actually relies on and it cannot then be drawn over — say which, and keep `no two boxes are drawn on top of each other` green after EVERY event, on both streams. Re-run `what-moves-and-how-far` and give me the new table beside the old one (moves, row changes, furthest, on both streams). If nearest-free-row makes anything worse on the recording, say so plainly and keep whichever rule moves tiles least overall — one rule, not a special case per map.
2. Make the docstrings and `theSettle.test.ts`'s row test say the rule as it now is: *a tile keeps its row while the map grows, unless the arrows send it into a column where that row is taken; then it takes the nearest free row.* Name the test for that second half in plain words.
3. Give me, in your report, the exact sentence(s) record 0024's clause 1 and INV-workbench.64's clause 1 should gain, with your measurements dated and attributed (how many times on each stream, how far, and the 140 px overlap the literal rule produced) — I will place them on the records' branch; you still must not edit a record or `streaming-growth.md`.
4. `frontend/src/keyboard/keys.ts:59` (*"Tiles do not move…"*) — leave it; I will carry that one.

Then `npm run check` once through the queue, and report only: the new table, the sentences for the record, what changed in `git diff --stat HEAD~N`, and anything that got worse. Do not run playwright; I run the browser suite after you report.

The settle is built and I've checked it: 202 layout and stream tests pass, types are clean, and the settled recording reads left to right in its pictures. I have not run its browser suite yet, and I've sent it back for one refinement.

**What it does**
- A tile's row stays pinned while a run is going. Its column is re-read from the arrows on every pass, and the whole map tidies once when the run stops, in the same frame the view re-frames.
- The agent wrote its tests before the fix. On the old code, four of nine arrows pointed backwards on your kept Verify run; with the fix, none do at any event.
- It moves fewer tiles than the five you accepted: 2 moves on the Verify run while it grows, and 3 on the recording.
- The zoom buttons no longer sit over the bottom-left tile at 1280×800.

**Test fixture**
The events of one paid Verify run are now committed as a test fixture (about 30 kB, with a README saying what it is and that nothing replays it). This is the call the earlier session took for you, and you can still overturn it.

**Where record 0024 is wrong**
- Record 0024 says a tile *never* changes row. When the arrows send a tile into a column where its row is already taken, it has to go somewhere.
- The literal rule drew one claim 140 px on top of another. The agent instead had the tile slide to the first free row below: twice on your Verify run, once on the recording.
- On your run that slide threw the Brent tile 392 px down when a free row sat 48 px up. I've sent it back to take the nearest free row, keep the no-overlap test passing after every event on both streams, and re-measure.
- I'll write the exception into the record with those measurements.

**What it could not fix**
- At 1600×1000 the stored map nearly touches the panel. The map is 1252 px wide in a 1264 px stage, so any real margin would cut the map off instead. That needs a narrower panel or a lower zoom floor, and that choice is yours.
- The key sheet still says *"Tiles do not move"*, which is now untrue during a run. I'll correct it when I assemble the batch.

**Lanes still running**
- the panel switcher
- the far-zoom range fix
- the three live-activity lanes
- the settle refinement

The colour lane is verified. I'm still waiting on you for the probe-script question.

## The new table, beside the old

Both streams, folded event by event through the app's own layering, layout engine and reading-back. *Row changes* are while the map is growing; the bracket is the furthest single row change.

| | moves / arrivals | furthest move | row changes | at the settle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Verify run**, first-free-row-below | 2 / 2 | 891 px | **2** (392 px) | 4 tiles, 738 px |
| **Verify run**, nearest-free-row | 2 / 2 | **801 px** | **1** (**48 px**) | 4 tiles, **498 px** |

| **Recording**, nearest-free-row | 3 / 2 | **400 px** | **0** | 18 tiles, **1 432 px** |

**Nothing got worse on either stream.** Same number of moves on the same arrivals; every distance shorter; the recording now has **no row change at all** while it grows, so record 0024's clause 1 holds on it literally. The Verify run's one remaining row change is the Brent tile going **48 px up** instead of 392 px down, on the same arrival that moves it 800 px right. The settle got shorter too, because the map it settles from is tidier.

**Reserved rectangles are not free room, and the 48 px case does not need them to be.** The obstacle in that case *is* a rectangle (`skeleton:B7ZC`), and what the tile relies on is being allowed to go **up** — it lands above the rectangle, with the full column gap between them, and the rectangle does not move. A rectangle is a box like any other in both the placing and the checking. `test_no_two_boxes_are_drawn_on_top_of_each_other` is green after **every** event of both streams, rectangles counted.

One rule, no special case per map: nearest free row, ties down, for every box that is not staying exactly where it was — movers and new arrivals alike.


One commit, `939707d`. `readPositions`'s slide loop is replaced by `nearestFreeRow`, which has its own docstring; `readPositions`' and `theSettle.test.ts`'s docstrings now state the rule with its exception. Two new tests on **built** inputs — `test_a_tile_sent_into_a_taken_row_takes_the_nearest_free_row` (it goes up, and nearer than the downward alternative, and the rectangle is neither moved nor drawn over) and `test_a_tie_between_two_free_rows_goes_down` (with the tie asserted to be a real tie first). 374 → 376 tests. `ARCHITECTURE.md` needed no edit: its figures are the move counts, which did not change.

Clause 1 currently ends *"…are pinned from the moment it is first drawn and are never taken from it while the map grows."* After that sentence:

> **With one exception, and it is the arrows' doing.** When a later arrow sends a tile into a column where the row it holds is already taken, it takes the **nearest free row** in that column — its own row whenever that row is free, and otherwise the closest one that is, up or down, with a tie going down, which is reading order. Clause 1's first sentence ends *"…has the identical vertical position after it, and its order within its column is unchanged"*. Insert before the em-dash that follows, or as its own sentence after it:

> — **unless that event moved its column and the row it held is taken there, and then it has the nearest free row in its new column**: its own row when that row is free, otherwise the closest free row up or down, a tie going down. Measured 2026-09-22 on both streams through the app's own layout code: **once on the live Verify run, by 48 pixels; never on the committed recording.** The exception is not a softening of the promise but the price of keeping it: with the row held regardless, the recording draws one claim **140 pixels on top of another**, which INV-workbench.79 and the visual checklist both forbid outright. A reserved rectangle is a box for this purpose — never room to be drawn over — and in the one measured case the tile passes **above** the rectangle rather than through it.

And, wherever that clause names its tests, add `test_a_tile_sent_into_a_taken_row_takes_the_nearest_free_row` and `test_a_tie_between_two_free_rows_goes_down`.

Nothing measured. Two things to know rather than faults:

- **`nearestFreeRow` now applies to newly arriving tiles too**, not only to movers, so a late arrival may take a free row *above* the boxes already in its column where it previously always went below. No test noticed, on either real stream or on the built maps — but it is a behaviour change to a path that predates this branch, and the browser run is where it would show.
- The commit message of `65e6db8` still describes the first-free-row-below rule and its 392 px cost. It is superseded by `939707d`, not rewritten, as you asked.

## What I built

**`stream/events.ts` + the reader.** The ninth event, `activity`, hand-typed from the shapes sheet exactly as the other eight are (`about` / `kind` / `text`). The grammar is split as the analysis asked: `StreamEvent` stays *the eight a recording holds*, `ReadEvent` gains the ephemeral ninth, and `generate.ts` matches on `NAMES_A_LIVE_RUN_MAY_SEND` so a name this build knows is never counted as one it does not. **A tenth name is still ignored without error and is pinned** — `generate.test.ts::test_an_activity_line_is_read_as_itself_and_a_tenth_name_still_is_not` and `growth.test.ts::test_a_tenth_name_is_still_ignored_without_error_now_that_there_are_nine`.

**`stream/growth.ts`.** Folding `activity` writes one field, `activity`, and nothing else — pinned by `expect({ ...after, activity: grown.activity }).toEqual(grown)`. Latest of each kind wins, never a list. Clearing: an accepted proposal clears the lines whose `about` names the call it answers (the sources of the arrows it brought; a proposal hanging off nothing is the opening call coming back); a refusal clears both; a stop clears everything; a line arriving after the end hands the same object back.

**An `activity` line is NOT an arrival for the seconds counter.** If it were, the strip would read *1 s* continuously through a three-minute call while nothing whatever reached the map — the screen that looks busy while nothing happens, which is the thing that counter exists to prevent. Kent's *"know the tool is alive"* is answered by the lines themselves changing in front of him; the number answers a different question, how long this call has been out. **So I changed the words, not the meaning:** `nothing new on the map for N s`. That keeps them true now that something else on the strip does change. The helper is `growth.ts::onlyTheStripChanged`, called from one line in `GenerationScreen`. The words also change on `MapScreen`'s strip (the *asking* state), where they are still true; I did not edit that file.

**A refusal now names what the model proposed, on the strip.** `whatChanged` said *"A proposal was refused. <rule's sentence>"* — a rule's sentence with nothing attached. I proved it fails loudly: with a `katalyst__engine__events__Activity` key present, `tsc` errors naming that key and telling you to delete the block. **At the join: delete it and pin `Activity` to the generated shape the way `Receipt` is pinned above.**

  readonly replaying: boolean;
